title: The staff and the shining hand
word: The staff and the shining hand
hook: his staff becomes a snake and his hand comes out white and shining: two signs

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fire on the mountain, and a man told to take off his sandals. Your line was you are in a sacred valley. Did you stop once and feel your feet? Day forty-nine, the end of the week.

Look down at your hands right now. What's in them? A phone, probably. A coffee. A steering wheel, hopefully not. Whatever it is, you stopped noticing it a long time ago. It's just what you carry. Musa is still standing barefoot in the sacred valley. He's just been told who God is, and that he's been chosen. And the next thing he hears isn't a thunderclap or a list of orders. It's a question, almost casual, the kind a friend asks. And it's about the thing in his hand. Today: the staff and the shining hand.
screen: `WHAT'S IN YOUR HANDS?` → `STILL BAREFOOT IN THE VALLEY.` → `A QUESTION, NOT AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha. In Pickthall's old translation: "And what is that in thy right hand, O Moses?" Of course Allah knows what it is. So why ask? Many commentators say the question was meant to make Musa look closely at something ordinary, so he'd know exactly what it was before it changed. And Musa answers at length. It's my staff. I lean on it. I knock leaves down with it for my sheep. And I have other uses for it too. Some commentators smile at that long answer: a man who's just been spoken to by his Lord, and who doesn't want the conversation to end. Then: throw it down. He does, and it's a snake, moving fast. Take it, and don't be afraid; We'll return it to how it was. Then the second sign: put your hand under your arm, and it will come out white, without any harm. The Qur'an adds that phrase, without any harm, so no one mistakes it for an illness. It's light, not sickness. Two signs, and both begin with what he already has. A shepherd's stick. His own hand. Nothing is brought down from the sky. The ordinary thing, looked at properly, turns out to be enough for the mission. And that's the whole week. A mother's hands letting go of a chest. A queen's arms. A sister who spoke up. A blow Musa regretted. A bucket at a well. A fire on a mountain. And now a staff. Seven days, and most of the turning points were in someone's hands.
screen: `WHAT IS THAT IN THY RIGHT HAND?` · `MY STAFF: I LEAN ON IT.` · `A SNAKE, THEN A STAFF AGAIN.` · `A HAND, SHINING, WITHOUT HARM.` · then, large: `TWO SIGNS, FROM WHAT HE HAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at what's in your hand. Set the phone face down for a moment, or keep it, and really look at it. Or look at your empty hand. Turn it over. See the lines, the knuckles, the small scar you forgot you had. Then ask the question, the way it was asked in the valley: what is this? And answer it honestly, at length if you like, like Musa. What does it do for you? What else could it be used for? If you pray, you can offer what's in your hand to Allah. The bell holds the time.
The staff and the shining hand. Two signs, made from a shepherd's stick and his own hand. Today's word.
screen: `THE STAFF AND THE SHINING HAND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what's in your right hand? Once today, notice what you're holding, and use it on purpose, for someone. Day forty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims count the staff and the shining hand among the signs, ayat, given to Musa, and the story is often told to show how Allah works through ordinary things.

fork.setup: you're Musa, barefoot in the sacred valley. a voice asks: what is that in your right hand? what do you say?
options: it's my staff. I lean on it, and I have other uses for it.
fork.reveal: he answers at length, and some commentators say it's because he didn't want the conversation to end. then: throw it down.

original.note: Arabic: staff, the shepherd's stick Musa leaned on, from Qur'an 20:18.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic trick with a stick.
what it means: two signs, the staff and the shining hand, both made from what Musa already had, given before he goes to Pharaoh.
what a scholar hears: 20:22 adds min ghayri su', "without any harm," so the white hand is not read as disease; commentators say the question in 20:17 was to make him look closely first.

sources.quoted: And what is that in thy right hand, O Moses?

notes: Quotation of 20:17 from Pickthall 1930 given from memory; please verify the exact wording against the 1930 text.
Commentary points (why Allah asks; Musa's long answer out of love of the conversation) stated as 'many/some commentators say'. Confirm.
'Put your hand under your arm' paraphrases 20:22 (idmum yadaka ila janahika), often rendered 'to your side'. Confirm.
